teaching.causalExplanation: Remember what a shortest path is. It's the path with the least total weight, and here the weights are kilometres. Every edge's weight said kilometres, so kilometres are all the method could see. But kilometres aren't the only thing that matters on a real trip. Say the toll road from A to B costs money, and the driver wants to avoid it. Take that edge away, and look again. Now the shortest path is A, C, D, twelve plus nine, twenty-one kilometres. That's only three kilometres longer, with no toll. For this driver, the longer path is the best path. The shortest path was right about distance, and wrong about what the driver cared about. Here's another. Two routes run between the same two towns. Route X is twelve kilometres through town, at fifty kilometres an hour. Route Y is fifteen kilometres on a motorway, at a hundred kilometres an hour. Route X is shorter. But time is distance divided by speed. Twelve divided by fifty is nought point two four of an hour, fourteen point four minutes. Fifteen divided by a hundred is nought point one five of an hour, nine minutes. The longer route is quicker by more than five minutes. So the weights you choose decide the answer. Weight the edges by distance, and route X wins. Weight them by time, and route Y wins. Lots of real things can make the shortest path a poor choice. A road might flood after heavy rain, or be closed for roadworks, so it isn't there at all. A bike route might be the shortest, but climb a steep hill, when a slightly longer path runs along the flat. A path might be quickest, but unsafe at night, or have no footpath. Traffic can turn a short road into a slow one at peak hour. In every case, the network's weights only measure one thing. When something else matters, the best path can be longer. That's why you should always ask what the weights measure, before you trust a shortest path.

scenes.teachingReason: Lots of real things can make the shortest path a poor choice. A road might flood after heavy rain, or be closed for roadworks, so it isn't there at all. A bike route might be the shortest, but climb a steep hill, when a slightly longer path runs along the flat. A path might be quickest, but unsafe at night, or have no footpath. Traffic can turn a short road into a slow one at peak hour. In every case, the network's weights only measure one thing. When something else matters, the best path can be longer. That's why you should always ask what the weights measure, before you trust a shortest path.

scenes.teachingReason: Now the second part of the idea. A shortest path isn't always inside a minimum spanning tree either. Here's a tiny network. A to B is three, B to C is three, and A to C is five. The minimum spanning tree takes the two threes, for six, and leaves out A to C, because it would close a loop. It's the only minimum spanning tree this network has. But the shortest path from A to C is the direct edge, five, and that edge isn't in the tree at all. If you could only use the tree, the trip from A to C would be six, through B. A minimum spanning tree keeps the total cost of linking everyone as low as possible. It doesn't promise the shortest trip between any two particular places. Real cables do the same thing. A town's fibre laid as a minimum spanning tree can send data from one tower to its neighbour the long way round.
